planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring into gritty, humus-rich soil that drains sharply but never fully dries; set the crown shallow since this species naturally roots among moss and leaf litter rather than deep soil.

directions: This evergreen Himalayan species is unusual within its genus for carrying glossy leaves in true opposite pairs along arching stems rather than the alternate or whorled arrangement typical of most Solomon's seals. In the wild it often grows as an epiphyte or lithophyte on moss-covered trunks and rock faces in Manipur and neighboring Himalayan forests, so garden plantings do best in a free-draining woodland mix that still holds some moisture rather than heavy clay. Cream flowers streaked with purple dangle from the leaf axils in spring and are followed by red berries that persist attractively into winter. Grow beneath high deciduous canopy alongside ferns and hellebores, dividing congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring in cool, humus-rich woodland soil in partial shade; this cold-hardy species from the Russian Far East tolerates harsher winters than most garden Solomon's seals.

directions: Named for its sharply tapering leaf tips, Polygonatum acuminatifolium ranges from the Russian Far East and Manchuria through Korea and Japan into northern China, growing along the edges of cool temperate woodlands where winters are long and severe. Slender arching stems carry the paired, drooping, greenish-white flowers typical of the genus in late spring, followed by small dark berries. Its native origin among taiga-adjacent forests makes it noticeably more cold-tolerant than many of the Chinese and Himalayan Solomon's seals now common in cultivation. Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist soil beneath deciduous shade and leave undisturbed except for occasional division to control spread.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in cool, humus-rich, consistently moist soil in partial to full shade; this species resents drying out even briefly and benefits from a thick leaf-mold mulch.

directions: Native to the mountain forests of central China, this clump-forming woodlander carries broad, glossy, bright green leaves along gently arching stems. In late spring it produces relatively large, hanging, bell-shaped white flowers that are proportionally bigger than those of most other fairy bells, giving the species its name, and these are followed by blue-black fruit. It needs year-round humidity and a humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil to thrive, making it a good companion for hostas, hellebores, and ferns in a cool, sheltered woodland bed. Propagate by division in early spring rather than seed for reliable results.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled to full shade; unlike many chain ferns this species tolerates drier hillside sites once established.

directions: Found across southern Japan, southern China, Taiwan, Vietnam, and northeastern Thailand, this chain fern grows on dry hill slopes in evergreen forest, a notably drier habitat than most Woodwardia species favor. A stout, erect rhizome bears tufted stipes and monomorphic fronds with seven to twenty pairs of deeply lobed lateral pinnae, giving the foliage a finely cut, almost pinnate-fern texture. Because it naturally tolerates slope drainage better than its wetland-loving relatives, it suits a shaded woodland bank rather than a boggy streamside. Mulch well at planting and keep soil evenly moist through the first year or two while the rhizome establishes.
sources: Kew Science - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into organic-rich soil that stays reliably damp, such as a streamside bed or shaded bank; this species is a specialist of the wettest, darkest forest-floor niches and will not tolerate drying out.

directions: Endemic to New Zealand's North and South Islands, this small tufted fern forms low rosettes along streamsides, wet gullies, and the base of shaded rock faces in lowland to lower montane forest. Its fronds are dimorphic: leathery, prostrate sterile fronds with toothed, rounded leaflets lie close to the ground, while narrower, upright fertile fronds rise above them to release spores. It hybridizes with the closely related Blechnum chambersii where their ranges overlap, so plants grown from spore in mixed collections may show intermediate traits. Site it in the dampest, darkest corner of a shade garden or fernery and keep the organic-rich soil constantly moist to mimic its forest-floor habitat.
sources: University of Auckland - New Zealand Plants
Kew Science - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in a free-draining, humus-rich mix in partial shade; in the wild this species often grows epiphytically on moss-covered trunks and rock outcrops, so avoid heavy, waterlogged soil.

directions: Ranging through the montane forests of southwestern China and across the Himalaya into Bhutan, northeastern India, Myanmar, and Nepal, this Solomon's seal grows at elevations up to nearly 9,000 feet, often rooted on moss-covered trees or rock outcrops rather than open ground. Its arching stems are distinctively spotted with lilac, and the small, urn-shaped flowers are white to greenish, likewise flecked with lilac, dangling in pairs beneath the foliage in the manner typical of the genus. Where winters are mild it holds its foliage through much of the year, giving longer seasonal interest than many deciduous Solomon's seals. Plant in a sheltered, well-drained woodland spot and mimic its epiphytic habit by avoiding soil that stays saturated for long periods.
